items.prompt: A subscriber's endpoint answers 503 to a webhook POST. CallWebhookJob was enqueued with { retryLimit: 3 }. What happens next?
items.answer: An audit event records the failure, and BullMQ never retries it
distractors: BullMQ retries the job up to 3 more times, then marks it failed
The job is moved to a dead-letter queue for a manual replay
The whole fan-out job reruns and re-matches the subscriptions
items.explanation: callWebhook wraps the POST in try/catch; the catch inserts a WEBHOOK_RESPONSE_EVENT audit row with success: false and does not rethrow. The job therefore completes normally, so BullMQ never sees a failure and retryLimit: 3 is dead configuration. No dead-letter path exists, and the fan-out job is not rerun.

items.prompt: A record mutation commits, and the server process crashes before the event batch is enqueued. Per ADR-010, what becomes of the event?
items.answer: It is lost for good, as no outbox row was written with the change
distractors: It is re-emitted at startup from Postgres's write-ahead log
It is sent later by a relay that polls the database for unsent event rows
It is rebuilt by the audit timeline the next time it is read
items.explanation: Emission happens in-process after the mutation, through workspace-event-emitter. There is no transactional outbox and no relay, so nothing durable records the pending event; a crash in that window loses it with no trace. That is the first half of ADR-010's 'at-most-once, twice over'.

items.prompt: When a webhook has a secret, what does callWebhook feed into the HMAC-SHA256 that produces X-Twenty-Webhook-Signature?
items.answer: The timestamp, a colon and the JSON payload without the secret
distractors: The JSON payload alone, with the secret field still included in it
The nonce and the payload, joined together by a colon
The target URL followed by the timestamp in seconds
items.explanation: generateSignature runs createHmac('sha256', secret).update(`${timestamp}:${JSON.stringify(payload)}`). The payload passed is payloadWithoutSecret, and the timestamp is the X-Twenty-Webhook-Timestamp header value, Date.now() in milliseconds. The nonce and URL are not signed.

items.prompt: A webhook was created without a secret. Which X-Twenty-Webhook-* headers does its POST carry?
items.answer: None, as all three are set only when a secret exists
distractors: All three, with the signature computed using an empty secret
Timestamp and nonce, but no signature since there is no key
Only the signature header, built from the workspace's API key
items.explanation: The headers object starts with Content-Type only, and the Timestamp, Signature and Nonce headers are all assigned inside if (secret) { ... }. Without a secret none of them is sent, so the receiver has nothing to verify.

items.prompt: Could a consumer use X-Twenty-Webhook-Nonce to recognise a redelivered event?
items.answer: No, as callWebhook draws 16 fresh random bytes for every POST
distractors: Yes, as the nonce is derived from the event id and webhook id
Yes, as the nonce is stored and reused on each retry attempt
No, as the nonce is only sent for events of type *.deleted
items.explanation: The nonce is crypto.randomBytes(16).toString('hex') at call time, so two deliveries of the same event carry different nonces. ADR-010 notes the payload carries no delivery-attempt identifier; a real idempotency key would have to be stable per (event, webhook).

items.prompt: An event batch named company.updated reaches CallWebhookJobsJob. Which operation patterns does it match webhooks against?
distractors: company.updated and *.* only, as other wildcards are not read
company.updated, company.* and *, but not *.updated
company.*, *.updated and *.*, but not the exact name
items.explanation: The job splits the batch name into nameSingular and operation and builds operationsToMatch = [`${nameSingular}.${operation}`, `*.${operation}`, `${nameSingular}.*`, '*.*']. A webhook matches when its operations include any one of them. A bare '*' is not in the list.

items.prompt: One event batch matches 45 webhook deliveries. How many CallWebhookJob jobs does CallWebhookJobsJob enqueue?
items.answer: 3 jobs, of 20, 20 and 5 deliveries, each with retryLimit 3
distractors: 45 jobs, one for each delivery, so each can retry on its own
1 job holding all 45 deliveries, run under one Promise.all
5 jobs of 9 deliveries each, as the chunk size adapts to load
items.explanation: WEBHOOK_JOBS_CHUNK_SIZE is 20, and the job loops over chunk(webhookEvents, 20), adding one CallWebhookJob per chunk with { retryLimit: 3 }. 45 deliveries give chunks of 20, 20 and 5. The size is a fixed constant.

items.prompt: A developer 'fixes' retries by rethrowing in callWebhook's catch. In a 20-delivery chunk, one POST fails. What does ADR-010 warn will happen?
items.answer: The whole chunk is retried, so successful deliveries go out again
distractors: Only the failed delivery is retried, as BullMQ tracks each one apart
The chunk is dropped, as Promise.all rejects before any POST
Nothing changes, since the fan-out job catches the rethrow
items.explanation: handle() runs the chunk with Promise.all, so one rejection fails the whole job, and a BullMQ retry re-runs every delivery in it, including the 19 that already succeeded. ADR-010 says correct retries need per-delivery jobs or idempotency keys. The POSTs have all started by the time Promise.all rejects.

items.prompt: How long does callWebhook wait for a subscriber's endpoint before the POST fails?
items.answer: 5 seconds, set by timeout 5_000 on the axios post call
distractors: 30 seconds, the default timeout of the shared HTTP client
10 minutes, the job's start-to-close limit in the queue
No limit; the POST waits until the socket is closed
items.explanation: The call is axiosClient.post(url, payload, { headers, timeout: 5_000 }). A slow endpoint therefore fails after 5 s, lands in the catch, and, as with any failure, is recorded and not retried. ADR-010 also lists the 5s timeout.

items.prompt: ADR-005: why can a service using twenty-orm not forget the deletedAt IS NULL filter, even on joined relations?
items.answer: The query-builder subclasses inject it into every query they build
distractors: A Postgres row-level security policy hides rows that are trashed
A lint rule fails the build when a query lacks the deletedAt filter
Trashed rows are moved to a separate archive schema right away
items.explanation: ADR-005: per-operation query-builder subclasses (select, insert, update, delete, soft-delete) inject schema resolution, permission predicates and default deletedAt IS NULL filtering, including on joined relations, so a caller cannot forget them. RLS was rejected, and trashed rows stay in place until trash cleanup.

items.prompt: ADR-005 considered Postgres row-level security for permissions. Why was it rejected?
items.answer: Policies would have to be regenerated on each metadata change
distractors: RLS cannot express field-level permissions on a custom object
Postgres RLS is not available on the managed databases in use
RLS policies would leak each workspace's schema name to clients
items.explanation: The ADR says policies would have to be generated and migrated per metadata change, on top of ADR-004's already nontrivial DDL engine, and that debugging authz inside the database at this level of dynamism is worse than in application code. Availability and leaks are not the reasons given.

items.prompt: ADR-007 translates coded exceptions at each protocol boundary. What does it say happens in background jobs, which have no such boundary?
items.answer: Throwing or catching becomes a delivery-semantics decision
distractors: Exceptions in jobs are turned into HTTP 500 responses for the queue
Jobs reuse the GraphQL exception hooks to translate their codes
Jobs may only throw bare Error, which the queue always retries
items.explanation: The negative consequences: in background jobs there is no protocol boundary, so the throw/catch decision silently becomes a delivery-semantics decision, and the sharpest example is ADR-010, where a swallowing catch disables retries. There is no HTTP response for a queue job, and bare Errors are a legacy pattern, not a rule.

items.front: Why does ADR-010 call webhook delivery 'at-most-once, twice over'?
items.back: Two independent gaps: (1) events are emitted in-process after commit with no transactional outbox, so a crash between commit and enqueue loses them; (2) callWebhook catches every delivery failure without rethrowing, so BullMQ never retries and retryLimit: 3 never fires.

items.front: ADR-005: what does twenty-orm push into query construction, and what is the single sanctioned entry point?
items.back: repository/workspace.repository.ts is the one entry point for record reads and writes. Its query-builder subclasses inject schema resolution, permission predicates (permissions.utils.ts) and default deletedAt IS NULL filtering, including on joins, and Postgres errors are translated into typed exceptions before they escape.

items.front: ADR-007's three tiers of error handling?
items.back: 1. Domain code throws typed, coded exceptions owned by each module; raw Postgres errors are converted inside the data layer. 2. Boundaries translate codes to protocol semantics (REST exception filter, GraphQL hooks). 3. Reporting is centralized behind a driver interface (Sentry or console), so where exceptions go is deployment configuration.

items.front: What harm does ADR-010 list for today's webhook delivery, and what bounded project fixes it?
items.back: Any consumer blip (deploy, 503, timeout) silently drops events; worker crashes drop them with no trace; retryLimit: 3 misleads readers into assuming at-least-once; failures are recorded in audit rows that nothing consumes, so customers find the loss. Fix: outbox, per-delivery idempotency keys, rethrow, dead-letter alerting.
